slides.title: Triglycerides
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood (venous sample)  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: The test helps assess the risk of heart disease, stroke and other artery conditions such as peripheral arterial disease, and helps monitor heart conditions and risk-lowering treatment. It is usually part of a lipid profile; high triglycerides with high LDL and/or low HDL can increase risk.
High triglycerides usually cause no symptoms, so routine testing helps find them before they harm health.

Physiology: Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood that the body uses for energy. Extra calories are turned into triglycerides and stored in fat cells; when energy is needed, cells release them into the bloodstream to fuel the muscles.

slides.title: Triglycerides
bullets: High: High triglycerides are very common and have many possible causes: a diet rich in fat, sugar and simple carbohydrates, too little exercise, kidney or liver disease, thyroid disease, poorly controlled diabetes, overweight or obesity, alcohol use disorder, inherited conditions and certain medicines (such as diuretics and some medicines for breast cancer and HIV).

High: Higher-than-normal triglycerides may mean a higher risk of heart disease, stroke and other artery conditions, and they also raise the risk of metabolic syndrome. Very high levels increase the risk of acute (sudden) pancreatitis in adults and children.
Low: Triglyceride levels that are too low are very uncommon.

slides.title: Triglycerides
bullets: Pre-analytics: Fasting (no food or drink) for 9 to 12 hours before the blood draw may be required; the provider says whether it is needed and gives any other instructions.

Limitations: Guidelines for children and teens differ from those for adults. With borderline results, the provider may order an apolipoprotein B (apo B) test to better understand the risk of heart and blood vessel problems.

slides.title: Non-HDL cholesterol
slides.eyebrow: Lipids · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Blood  ·  Units: mg/dL, mmol/L
What it is used for: Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol; it may be reported with lipid (lipoprotein) panel results.
Non-HDL includes LDL and other types of cholesterol such as VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein), so it gives a better picture of all the “bad” cholesterol types that can raise heart risk.

slides.eyebrow: Lipids · Reference values and decision limits
rows: Coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk equivalents (10-year CHD risk above 20%)
2 or more risk factors (10-year risk 20% or lower)
Very high risk with high triglycerides

slides.title: Non-HDL cholesterol
bullets: Limitations: The numbers that are best for a person may depend on age, race, blood pressure, weight, family history and more, so the lipid levels that are best for them are checked with the provider.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
bullets: High cholesterol is found from medical and family history, a physical exam and a blood test (lipid panel). Screening in healthy people: start at ages 9–11 and repeat every 5 years; every 5 years at 20–65 (every 1–2 years for men 45–65 and women 55–65); yearly after 65.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: The main source of cholesterol buildup and blockages in arteries; high LDL raises risk.
Helps decrease cholesterol blockages in arteries; low HDL is a concern.
High triglycerides may signal a higher risk of coronary heart disease.
The main screening test is a lipid panel; fasting for 8–12 hours may be requested.
Total cholesterol minus HDL; may also be reported.
Not part of a routine lipid panel; largely inherited and stable over life. May be ordered with a family history of stroke or early heart disease, or if family history is unknown.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
rows: Higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease.
HDL < 40 mg/dL (≈1.0 mmol/L) in men or < 50 mg/dL (≈1.3 mmol/L) in women
May mean a higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease; may lead to a statin prescription.

slides.title: Dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk
bullets: Individual target levels are set by the clinician based on risk factors. mmol/L values are converted from mg/dL (approximate).

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
bullets: You may have metabolic syndrome if you have three or more of the listed conditions. Waist size, blood pressure and blood tests (fasting glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides) are assessed.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
rows: Blood glucose after fasting for 8–12 hours.
One criterion is consistently high triglycerides.
One criterion is low HDL cholesterol.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
rows: One metabolic syndrome criterion (harmonized cut point ≥ 150 mg/dL; the NHLBI page says “consistently more than 150”).
HDL < 40 mg/dL (≈1.0 mmol/L) in men or < 50 mg/dL (≈1.3 mmol/L) in women
Fasting glucose ≥ 100 mg/dL (≈5.6 mmol/L) or taking glucose-lowering medicine
One criterion — high blood sugar: 100–125 mg/dL (≈5.6–6.9 mmol/L) means high blood sugar or prediabetes; ≥ 126 mg/dL (≈7.0 mmol/L) may mean diabetes.
Waist > 40 inches in men / > 35 inches in women; blood pressure consistently ≥ 130/85
Non-lab criteria; waist thresholds may vary by race and ethnicity.

slides.title: Metabolic syndrome
bullets: For children the clinician sets the measures and cut-offs. mmol/L values are converted from the source’s units (approximate).

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: optimal <1.7 (150 mg/dL); mildly raised 1.7–2.2 (150–199); high 2.3–5.6 (200–499); very high >5.6 (>500) – risk of pancreatitis mmol/L (from mg/dL by dividing by 88.5)
Applicability limit of the Friedewald formula
LDL = TC − HDL − TG/2.2 (mmol/L) or TG/5 (mg/dL); not used when TG >4.5 mmol/L (>400 mg/dL) mmol/L

slides.title: Besides cardiovascular risk, which acute condition does the source link to very high triglyceride levels?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source says very high triglycerides increase the risk of acute pancreatitis in adults and children.

Basis: MedlinePlus: very high triglyceride levels increase the risk of acute pancreatitis.

slides.title: Why does the source stress routine triglyceride testing?
options: High triglycerides always cause abdominal pain, so the test is needed to confirm the cause of the pain
Triglycerides can only be measured during an acute illness such as pancreatitis
High triglycerides usually cause no symptoms, so testing finds them before they cause harm
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. This is the reason the source gives for routine testing.

Basis: MedlinePlus: high triglycerides usually cause no symptoms, so routine testing is important.

slides.title: How is non-HDL cholesterol obtained?
options: The sum of LDL cholesterol and HDL cholesterol
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. MedlinePlus and NHLBI both define non-HDL this way.

Basis: MedlinePlus and NHLBI: non-HDL = total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol.

slides.title: Why can non-HDL cholesterol give a broader picture than LDL alone?
options: It includes LDL and other cholesterol types such as VLDL
It also counts HDL, the “good” cholesterol, as part of its total
It measures only triglycerides, not cholesterol
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. According to the source, this is why it gives a better picture of the “bad” cholesterol types.

Basis: MedlinePlus: non-HDL includes LDL and other cholesterol types such as VLDL and gives a better picture of the “bad” types.

slides.title: On what is the biological role of triglycerides based:
Enzymes involved in the hydrolysis of triglycerides:
Turbidity of blood serum is associated with:
Biological role of unsaturated fatty acids:
Methods of determining triglycerides?
bullets: 1. The main method is enzymatic: lipase hydrolyzes TG to glycerol and fatty acids; glycerol is oxidized by glycerol kinase and glycerol-3-phosphate oxidase to produce H2O2; with peroxidase a colored product (GPO-PAP, Trinder) is measured photometrically.
2. Free glycerol (for example heparin, glycerol-containing drugs, sample storage) falsely raises the result – a glycerol blank if needed.
3. Preanalytics: TG rises after a meal – a high result (or suspected pancreatitis) is rechecked fasting (≈10–12 hours); a lipemic sample interferes with other tests.
4. Interpretation: target <1.7 mmol/L (<150 mg/dL); at >5.6 mmol/L (500 mg/dL) the risk of acute pancreatitis rises sharply; with high TG the Friedewald formula is unsuitable.
5. Increase: secondary – diabetes, obesity, alcohol, hypothyroidism, CKD, drugs (estrogens, steroids); primary – familial hypertriglyceridemia, LPL/apoC-II deficiency.
